card.stem: A house built in the 1970s has an un-insulated solid concrete ground floor with a sand/cement fine screed finish.
card.questionText: Calculate the U-value of the concrete ground floor given the following data: Sand/cement fine screed thickness 60 mm; Concrete floor slab thickness 100 mm; Damp proof membrane (DPM) thickness 0.25 mm; Sand blinding thickness 50 mm; Hardcore thickness 225 mm; Subsoil thickness 300 mm. Thermal data of concrete ground floor: Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.104 m2 °C/W; Resistivity of fine screed (r) 0.710 m °C/W; Conductivity of concrete floor slab (k) 0.160 W/m °C; Conductivity of DPM (k) 0.250 W/m °C; Conductivity of sand blinding (k) 0.160 W/m °C; Conductivity of hardcore (k) 1.330 W/m °C; Conductivity of subsoil (k) 1.800 W/m °C.

rows.contextNote: The calculation set out in a table of material, conductivity or resistivity, thickness and resistance.

Seven resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (R = T × r for the screed): screed 0.060 × 0.710 = 0.0426; slab 0.100/0.160 = 0.625; DPM 0.00025/0.250 = 0.001; sand blinding 0.050/0.160 = 0.3125; hardcore 0.225/1.330 = 0.1692; subsoil 0.300/1.800 = 0.1667; internal surface 0.104 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance, the sum of R = 1.421 m²°C/W.
U = 1/Rt = 1 ÷ 1.421 = 0.704 W/m²K (1 mark for the formula).

(a) Calculate the U-value of the concrete ground floor given the following data: Sand/cement fine screed thickness 60 mm; Concrete floor slab thickness 100 mm; Damp proof membrane (DPM) thickness 0.25 mm; Sand blinding thickness 50 mm; Hardcore thickness 225 mm; Subsoil thickness 300 mm. Thermal data of concrete ground floor: Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.104 m2 °C/W; Resistivity of fine screed (r) 0.710 m °C/W; Conductivity of concrete floor slab (k) 0.160 W/m °C; Conductivity of DPM (k) 0.250 W/m °C; Conductivity of sand blinding (k) 0.160 W/m °C; Conductivity of hardcore (k) 1.330 W/m °C; Conductivity of subsoil (k) 1.800 W/m °C.

(b) Using the U-value of the concrete ground floor obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through the un-insulated concrete floor slab: Dimensions of floor 9.0 metres × 7.0 metres; Average internal temperature 20° C; Average external temperature of subsoil 5° C; Heating period 12 hours per day for 40 weeks per annum; Cost of oil 85 cent per litre; Calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 Watts 1 kJ per second.

(c) An insulated concrete ground floor is designed to prevent the penetration of radon gas through the floor and to meet the Passive House standard. Using notes and freehand sketches, show the typical design detailing for such a floor.

rows.contextNote: The calculation set out in a table of material, conductivity or resistivity, thickness and resistance.

Seven resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (R = T × r for the screed): screed 0.060 × 0.710 = 0.0426; slab 0.100/0.160 = 0.625; DPM 0.00025/0.250 = 0.001; sand blinding 0.050/0.160 = 0.3125; hardcore 0.225/1.330 = 0.1692; subsoil 0.300/1.800 = 0.1667; internal surface 0.104 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance, the sum of R = 1.421 m²°C/W.
U = 1/Rt = 1 ÷ 1.421 = 0.704 W/m²K (1 mark for the formula).
Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 0.704 × 63 × 15 = 665.28 watts (joules per second).
Heating period = 12 × 7 × 40 = 3,360 hours = 12,096,000 seconds.

rows.verbatim: litres of oil for one year
Passive insulated ground floor with radon barrier Notes
rows.contextNote: Such as: 25 mm screed on a 75 mm slab; 250–400 mm expanded polystyrene for U ≤ 0.15 W/m²K; a radon barrier; sand blinding and hardcore; a low-conductivity thermal block in the inner leaf; 300 mm cavity insulation.
A sketch of the floor and its junction with the wall, as in the scheme’s model detail.

card.questionText: The drawing shows an outline section through a portion of a single storey house of timber frame construction. The outer leaf is of rendered concrete block and the ground floor is an insulated solid concrete floor. Select any three locations from those circled on the sketch and show, using notes and freehand sketches, the typical design detailing which will prevent air leakage at each of the locations selected.

rows.contextNote: Any three of the four circled locations, each note 5 and sketch 5 = 10. Ground Floor: an airtightness membrane and butyl tape carried under the timber frame and bonded to the slab; mastic sealant under the skirting; mortar joints pointed and sealed; a service cavity so the barrier is not ruptured. Window Cill: the air barrier bonded to the DPC; joints at the window, window board and cill taped and sealed with mastic; a draught seal between the opening sash and the frame. Light Fittings: grommets around cables piercing the barrier; the barrier resealed with tape and mastic; no recessed lights, or enclosed casings; a service cavity where possible. Trapdoor: a gasket or draught seal along the batten; tape returned along the joist; a bolt compressing the seal; insulation on the back; a proprietary trapdoor with sealed rebates.

(b) It is proposed to install a Mechanical Heat Recovery with Ventilation (MHRV) system for a Passive House, as shown in the drawing. The location of the MHRV unit - M - in the utility room is shown. rows.contextNote: Any two of the three printed items, each note 5 and sketch 5 = 10. Building form: a compact form with a minimum of extensions, as heat is lost through the external surfaces; a surface-to-volume ratio of 0.7 or less. Indoor environment: relative humidity of 35–55% against respiratory illness, mould and dust mites; internal surfaces not below 12.6°C, preventing condensation. card.stem: “A sustainable ethos in building will require the consideration of environmental implications associated with design, construction and operation of buildings and neighbourhoods; and greater emphasis on the improvement of existing buildings. Most buildings are used for several decades, and many survive for centuries. As the community’s principal physical asset, getting good value requires that the building’s full life cycle be considered, avoiding short-sighted attempts to merely minimise initial cost.” THE GREEN VITRUVIUS – PRINCIPLES AND PRACTICE OF SUSTAINABLE ARCHITECTURAL DESIGN (2011) by Vivienne Brophy and J Owen Lewis (UCD). - Earthscan Ltd, 14a St Cross Street, London ECIN 8XA, UK
card.questionText: Discuss the above statement in detail.

rows.verbatim: Discussion – point 1 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: a sustainable ethos puts the environment at the heart of every design decision — doing more with less for longer, thinking globally and acting locally, with best practice the only acceptable standard.

rows.verbatim: Discussion – point 2 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: a whole-systems team approach at the design stage, with low embodied energy, renewable materials and life-cycle costing, and each building considered within its neighbourhood.

rows.verbatim: Discussion – point 3 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: buildings as the community’s principal asset — durable, beautiful and flexible; low initial cost brings higher lifetime costs. Three distinct, well-argued points are needed.
